articles.title: It’s official: Samsung Gallery now uses your Google storage to sync your photos and videos
articles.excerpt: Samsung's OneDrive replacement is Google.
articles.body: TL;DR Samsung has officially announced that its Gallery app can now sync photos and videos to users’ Google account storage. It lets you view synced photos and videos across Galaxy devices. The feature is rolling out to select Galaxy devices running One UI 9, and will roll out to more devices in phases. Samsung’s partnership with Microsoft OneDrive ended in late September , leaving a pretty big gap in Samsung Gallery’s cloud backup capabilities. Although we already knew the company was going to partner with Google for cloud storage, that’s now getting officially confirmed. Samsung today announced Gallery sync with Google storage to make it easier for users to back up their photos to the cloud and access them from anywhere.

articles.title: I hid 6 secret glitches in my agent's video game. They make it easier. Can it find them?
articles.excerpt: My agent can beat a platformer it has never seen. Flash is my open source agent for the terminal and the browser. One of its tools, play_realtime, lets the model write a tiny reflex: a JavaScript func…
articles.body: My agent can beat a platformer it has never seen. Flash is my open source agent for the terminal and the browser. One of its tools, play_realtime , lets the model write a tiny reflex : a JavaScript function that runs every single frame inside the page, reads the canvas pixels, and presses keys. The model can't think 60 times a second, so it writes the thing that can. To test it, Flash ships with Flash Dash : a little level built like a rhythm runner. A square runs right on its own. Spikes kill. Blue blocks are solid. An orange pad launches you. A cyan ring gives you a second jump in mid-air. Then a gate turns you into a ship you fly between pillars. The reference reflex beats it on the first try, from the pixels alone, in 21.11 seconds . That's a solved problem.

articles.title: A robot just built a structure autonomously in space for the 1st time ever
articles.excerpt: A robot built part of an antenna in orbit recently, showcasing skills that could potentially allow the assembly of space telescopes and other large structures off Earth.
articles.body: A robot just played Tinkertoys in space, assembling the first satellite structure ever made without a human touching the controls. The DARPA-funded project saw a robotic "truss builder" create a reflective antenna using Kapton film, composite fiber tubes and aluminum joints. The implications are huge for future missions, potentially opening up new possibilities to build — or fix — satellites in the final frontier. "This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space ," Sergio Pellegrino, an aerospace and civil engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement on Nov. 5 .

articles.title: Even a mechanical migration deserves a spec
articles.excerpt: Swapping Jest for Vitest is a mechanical migration. I still wrote a spec before touching a single test. The reason was simple: the design system already ran on Vite (Storybook included), and Jest with…
articles.body: Swapping Jest for Vitest is a mechanical migration. I still wrote a spec before touching a single test. The reason was simple: the design system already ran on Vite (Storybook included), and Jest with ts-jest kept a second transform pipeline alive just for tests. Consolidate, and get faster. The spec had three parts. Inventory. 68 test files. jest.fn in about 120 places across 30 files. jest.mock in 15. Fake timers in exactly one file. toBeInTheDocument used 219 times. I knew exactly what would break. Non-goals. No migrating legacy packages that have no tests. No root-level Vitest config until a second package gets tests. No swapping jsdom for happy-dom. And no behavior changes in the tests, only jest.* becoming vi.*. Definition of done.

Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30 , the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras. The ZWO Seestar S30 Plus is a new sub-$500 smart telescope with upgraded optics and dual 3.7MP cameras.

articles.title: Total solar eclipse 2027 vs 2028 — Which one should you choose, Egypt or Australia?
articles.excerpt: From six minutes of darkness in Egypt or totality over the Australian Outback, here are the pros and cons of the next two total solar eclipses.
articles.body: For those who want to experience a total solar eclipse, the next two years present the best kind of problem. On Aug. 2, 2027, the so-called "eclipse of the century " will sweep across southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, bringing more than six minutes of totality to parts of Egypt. Then, on July 22, 2028, another exceptionally long total solar eclipse will cross Australia, putting the remote Outback and Sydney Harbor in the path of the moon's dark central shadow before it reaches New Zealand's beautiful South Island. Both eclipses will be spectacular, and both will require careful planning, yet they promise very different experiences.

articles.title: NASA's twin ESCAPADE Mars probes slingshot around Earth in unprecedented double 'gravity assist'
articles.excerpt: NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long voyage to Mars, and are now ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet.
articles.body: Twin NASA spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long escapade, ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet. The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) spacecraft launched in November 2025 on the second-ever flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. But rather than head straight to Mars, the two spacecraft dawdled through a looping trajectory . Now, they are back in Earth's neighborhood where they tackled a crucial engine burn unusually close to Earth that — if all goes well — will set them on track for Mars . "No NASA mission has ever done this before," said Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and principal investigator of the ESCAPADE mission.
